cummo.pairwise: The 50-400-T64 and Cycloclasticus metabat_9342 subunit A proteins share 37% identity over 234 amino acids with each other.
cummo.short: its closest characterised relatives are the propane/ethane monooxygenases of Cycloclasticus, at about 48% identity
cummo.summary: The CuMMO subunit A of comebin_2576 is 81% identical to the one in the 50-400-T64 type genome (GCA_002162755.1). That genome is a MAG from a laboratory simulation of the Deepwater Horizon deep-sea oil plume, where the fastest-growing bacteria used short-chain alkanes (Hu et al. 2017, PNAS). The two genomes share about 81% average nucleotide identity over 60% of comebin_2576, so they are different species of the same genus. The type genome also carries the CuMMO and several cyclohexanone monooxygenases. Outside the genus, the closest references are the Cycloclasticus CuMMOs that oxidise propane, ethane and butane (48% at most). Next come methane monooxygenases (42%) and bacterial ammonia monooxygenases (41%); the archaeal amoA is unrelated (24%). So this is a separate, Porticoccaceae lineage of the CuMMO family, most likely a short-chain or sub-terminal alkane monooxygenase, and not a nitrifier or methanotroph enzyme. The Cycloclasticus metabat_9342 CuMMO is divergent too: about 50% identical to the known Cycloclasticus alkane CuMMOs and 50% to gammaproteobacterial pmoA. Identities this low cannot place it confidently within the family.
